market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: TVP vs. ground beef: nutrition compared

seo.title: TVP vs. ground beef: protein, fiber and fat
seo.meta_description: Compare textured soy protein with 90/10 ground beef using the same 20 g protein target.
seo.search_intent: Compare TVP and ground beef nutrition

excerpt: Dry TVP and raw ground beef contain very different amounts of water. Comparing enough of each to provide about 20 g protein makes the trade-offs clearer.
content_html:
TVP and ground beef can fill the same role in tacos, chili, or pasta sauce, but comparing 100 g with 100 g is misleading because TVP is sold dry while fresh beef contains much more water. A clearer comparison is to ask how much of each food provides about 20 g of protein.

Match the protein target first

Dry TVPRaw 90/10 ground beef
Amount for ~20 g protein~38 g~100 g
Calories~132~176
Protein~20 g~20 g
Fiber~6.7 g0 g
FatVery low before cooking~10 g

The large weight difference does not mean TVP is several times “more nutritious.” It mainly reflects dehydration. Once 38 g of TVP is rehydrated, it takes up much more water and volume.

Fiber is a fundamental difference

The protein-matched TVP portion contributes roughly 6–7 g fiber; beef contributes none. In a bowl of chili or pasta sauce, that can make a meaningful difference to the meal's total fiber.

Beef carries more fat in this comparison

Raw 90/10 ground beef provides about 10 g fat per 100 g, including roughly 4 g saturated fat. Plain defatted TVP starts very low in fat, although the final dish depends on the oil used during cooking.

A generous pour of oil can erase part of the calorie difference quickly, so the ingredient comparison should not be confused with the nutrition of the finished recipe.

The micronutrients are not interchangeable

Beef naturally supplies vitamin B12, zinc, and heme iron. Soy provides nonheme iron, magnesium, and other minerals, but unfortified TVP should not be treated as a natural B12 source.

Replacing beef with TVP therefore involves more than matching protein. A fully plant-based diet still needs a reliable source of vitamin B12.

Sodium depends on the product and seasoning

Plain TVP can start relatively low in sodium, but broth, soy sauce, seasoning packets, and ready-made meatless crumbles can raise it sharply. Fresh beef also starts fairly low and changes once salt and sauces are added.

Are they nutritionally equivalent?

They can replace each other in a recipe, but they are not nutritional copies. For the same protein target, the TVP example is lower in calories and fat and adds fiber; beef contributes B12, zinc, and heme iron. The useful question is which trade-off fits the rest of the meal.

faq.question: Does TVP have more protein?
faq.answer: Dry TVP is more concentrated; about 38 g dry here provides ~20 g protein, similar to 100 g raw 90/10 beef.

faq.question: Does TVP provide B12?
faq.answer: Not naturally in a dependable amount.
